extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of evolutionary theory, biology, sociology, and anthropology (Victorian-era scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the law of evolution framed as a general process in which systems (biological, social, linguistic, cultural) change from homogeneity toward heterogeneity, with examples and evidential discussion. The text explains mechanistic/observational indicators and cautions about paleontological inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation from homogeneity to heterogeneity in organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Each organism, during its evolution, passes from a state of homogeneity to a state of heterogeneity; the history of every plant and animal is one of increasing bulk accompanied by simultaneously-increasing differences among the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a general law (credited to Von Baer and Harvey) and described as the most conspicuous part of secondary re-distributions accompanying primary re-distribution. This principle is presented as universal across organisms and is the organizing idea for subsequent examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical differentiation within developing organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The chemical composition almost uniform in a germ gradually ceases to be uniform; compounds segregate, become diversely proportioned in different places, and produce new compounds by transformation or modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in plants albuminous and amylaceous matter give rise to chlorophyll in some places and cellulose in others; starch converts to sugar or gum in different locales; cellulose becomes wood or cork. In animals protein, fats, and salts become differently proportioned; accumulations lead to blood, nerve-tissue, cartilage, and bone. These progressive chemical differentiations initiate further unlikenesses by mixing in unlike ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minute structural differentiation (tissues and cells)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct tissues arise from originally similar granular protoplasm and cells, with subsequent secondary modifications producing sub-species of tissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vegetal protoplasm forming cells that flatten and unite to form outer layers, elongate into woody-fibre bundles, or develop spiral threads/reticulated frameworks to form vessels; leaf tissue re-differentiation into packed chlorophyll-cells and spongy lower strata. In animal embryos, repeated fission of superficial cells and their unions form outer layers and differentiated middle areas; many modifications produce classes and sub-classes of tissues composing organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological divergence of shape and organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Germs start as spheres and organs as buds or rounded lumps; from primordial uniformity there is divergence toward multiformity and complexity of contour—buds that are alike give rise to diverse organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: young leaves terminating shoots are central knobs bearing lateral knobs, each of which may grow into leaf, sepal, petal, stamen, carpel; limbs of Articulata begin similar and diverge (e.g., crab vs lobster); bird wings and legs bud out similarly but differentiate. The process: a first difference between two parts, then further differences within each, multiplying until adult complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats and standards for inferring historical increases in heterogeneity from the fossil record
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences about whether modern flora and fauna are more heterogeneous than ancient ones must account for fragmentary evidence, limited exposure of strata, preservational biases, and geological transformations that produce gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points raised: two-thirds of Earth's surface is water; many strata inaccessible or imperfectly explored; perishable lower organisms and metamorphosed strata; repeated discoveries of higher organisms in strata thought barren (negative evidence is weak); igneous action has destroyed older strata, so the 'oldest known' is not necessarily earliest. These considerations constitute a methodological caution in using paleontological records to assert progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanations and geological effects on apparent progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent succession from more homogeneous to more heterogeneous forms in strata can be accounted for by taphonomy, depositional environment, immigration, and large-scale geological subsidences and elevations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Paleozoic deposits being non-estuarine and unlikely to contain terrestrial vertebrate remains; later appearance of reptiles/birds/mammals could be due to immigration to newly uplifted continents; breaks in succession explained by subsidences/elevations. Counterarguments like 'persistent types' are answered by positing a pre-geologic era of unknown duration. The text emphasizes interpreting geological and fossil data in light of these processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paleontological facts that support gradual evolution toward heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite fragmentary evidence, some fossil facts are consistent with evolution from less to more heterogeneous forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited supportive facts: community of type between fossils of adjacent strata and between recent tertiary fossils and living creatures; discovery of intermediate forms (e.g., Palæotherium, Anoplotherium) indicating intermediate structural types; comparatively recent appearance of Man with greater heterogeneity—these make the fossil evidence more supportive than contradictory of evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human biological evolution: increased heterogeneity with civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: During human history the human organism has grown more heterogeneous among civilized divisions of the species; the species as a whole has become more heterogeneous by multiplication and differentiation of races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and indicators: relative development of limbs (Europeans have relatively longer, more massive legs than Papuans), increased cranial-to-facial bone ratio, larger cerebrum relative to subjacent ganglia suggesting more complex nervous system. Infant traits show resemblances; civilized developmental processes continue embryonic trend from homogeneous to heterogeneous. Ethnological divisions and recent examples (Anglo-Americans, emerging Australian variety) illustrate increasing heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social evolution: differentiation of governing vs governed and emergence of distinct institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Social masses differentiate from homogeneous aggregations into governing and governed parts, with subsequent differentiation of the governing into civil, religious, and ceremonial (manners) institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stages described: early chieftainship indistinct and shared; later hereditary rulers who cease self-provision and are served; religion and kingship closely associated (king as priest); religion and civil law diverge over time; manners/ceremonial usages originate from god-king practices and become generalized social customs. Titles and salutations evolve from obeisances to ordinary forms of address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social evolution: division of labour, class differentiation, and geographic/economic specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies progress from members doing the same tasks to minute divisions of labour among classes and to regional/national specialization of occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transition from hunter/producer families to caste/guild divisions and modern producing/distributing organizations; later, improved transit causes districts and nations to specialize (calico in one county, woollens in another, towns specialized in pottery, hardware, etc.); free trade promotes international specialization—an economic aggregation of the human race becoming ever more heterogeneous in functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural evolution: language development from simple to complex parts of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Language advances from simple forms (exclamation) through stages where nouns and verbs are primary, to differentiated parts of speech (auxiliaries, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, articles) and grammatical distinctions (mood, tense, person, number, case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that languages can be traced to a stage with only nouns and verbs; progressive multiplication of parts of speech increases heterogeneity. The author asserts English's superiority in part due to an extensive subdivision of functions in its grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic diversification: multiplication of words and languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of allied meanings differentiate into families and sub-families by modification and derivation, and languages themselves diverge into distinct tongues and dialects, increasing heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aboriginal names applied to broad classes become modified into names for chief divisions; formation of derivatives and compound terms produce many distinct words; language families (e.g., Indo-European) diverge by continuous processes into multiple languages and dialects, yielding lexicons of tens of thousands of unlike words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written and pictorial arts develop as appendages of architecture and theocratic government
rubrics_metrics.description: Written language, painting, and sculpture originate as appendages of architecture and are closely connected with theocratic governmental functions, serving governmental and religious purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cave paintings by wild races likely in sacred places; Egyptian and Assyrian mural paintings decorate temples/palaces and represent worship, triumphs of rulers, submission of subjects, and punishment of rebels. These arts were governmental appliances and products of arts revered as sacred mysteries.
